title: Anatomy of Uvea, Accomodation with its Anomalies

questions.sec: Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
questions.q: Match the uveal component with its uveal part and its inflammation — 1) Iris with pars plicata of the ciliary body 2) Pars plana of the ciliary body 3) Choroid … A) Intermediate uvea / intermediate uveitis B) Anterior uvea / anterior uveitis C) Posterior uvea / posterior uveitis
questions.exp: The components-of-uvea table pairs iris plus ciliary body pars plicata with anterior uvea (anterior uveitis), pars plana with intermediate uvea (intermediate uveitis) and choroid with posterior uvea (posterior uveitis). (Book p8)

questions.sec: Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
questions.q: The iris is pigmented because of which cell?
questions.exp: Anatomy of the iris: increased vascularity, pigmentation d/t melanocytes, and variable thickness. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
questions.q: The thickest part of the iris, which marks the boundary between its pupillary and ciliary zones, is the:
questions.exp: The iris figure labels the collarette as the thickest part and the boundary between the pupillary zone and the ciliary zone of the iris. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
questions.q: After blunt ocular trauma a patient shows a tear at the peripheral iris where it looks thinnest on gonioscopy. The book names this detachment of the iris:
questions.exp: The thinnest part of the iris is the root, labelled the site of iridodialysis (detachment of iris). (Book p8)

questions.sec: Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
questions.q: Match the iris muscle with its action and autonomic control — 1) Sphincter pupillae 2) Dilator pupillae … A) Mydriasis under sympathetic (excitatory) control B) Miosis under parasympathetic (inhibitory) control
questions.exp: Sphincter pupillae produces miosis under parasympathetic (inhibitory) control; dilator pupillae produces mydriasis under sympathetic (excitatory) control. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
questions.q: Match the sympathetic relay station of the dilator pathway with its order — 1) First order 2) Second order 3) Third order … A) Superior cervical ganglion to the eye along the internal carotid, ending in the long ciliary nerve B) Hypothalamus to the spinal cord's ciliospinal centre (C8-T1) C) Ciliospinal centre to the superior cervical ganglion, crossing the lung parenchyma
questions.exp: The sympathetic chain for the dilator: hypothalamus → 1° spinal cord ciliospinal centre (C8-T1) → 2° crossing lung parenchyma to the superior cervical ganglion → 3° along the internal carotid as the long ciliary nerve. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
questions.q: During resection of a Pancoast tumour the surgeon warns of damage to the sympathetic fibres heading to the superior cervical ganglion. Per the book's iris-supply table, the ocular consequence is:
opts: Paralysis of the inferior oblique muscle
Loss of sympathetic supply to the eye
Loss of parasympathetic supply to the sphincter
questions.exp: The book flags resection of a Pancoast tumour as a risk of damage to SCG fibres at the second-order step, producing loss of sympathetic supply to the eye. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
questions.q: Which statement about the final nerve supply of the iris muscles is FALSE per the book?
opts: The sphincter's final supply is the long ciliary nerve
The sphincter's post-ganglionic supply reaches it through the short ciliary nerve
The dilator's final supply is the long ciliary nerve
The parasympathetic route to the sphincter runs via the oculomotor nerve
questions.exp: Final nerve supply per the table: sphincter pupillae — infraorbital branch (to inferior oblique muscle) then short ciliary nerve (post ganglion); dilator pupillae — long ciliary nerve. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
questions.q: The book's oculomotor branch diagram lists the muscles of each division. All of the following are supplied by the INFERIOR branch of the oculomotor nerve EXCEPT:
opts: None of these three is inferior-branch supplied
questions.exp: Superior branch supplies superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris; inferior branch supplies inferior rectus and inferior oblique. (Book p9)

questions.sec: Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
questions.q: Horner's syndrome is defined in the book as:
opts: Oculoparasympathetic palsy of the ciliary ganglion (parasympathetic)
Sensory loss over the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal (V1)
questions.exp: Horner's syndrome (HS) is oculosympathetic palsy, i.e. paralysis of the sympathetic supply to the eye. (Book p9)

questions.sec: Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
questions.q: Match the Horner's neuron order with a listed cause — 1) First order (central) 2) Second order (preganglionic) 3) Third order (postganglionic) … A) Pancoast tumour, carotid and aortic aneurysm, neck lesions B) Cluster headache, internal carotid artery dissection, otitis media, cavernous sinus mass C) Brainstem lesions, syringomyelia, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, Wallenberg syndrome
questions.exp: First order (central, hypothalamus to ciliospinal centre C8-T1): brainstem lesions, syringomyelia, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, Wallenberg syndrome. Second order (preganglionic, to superior cervical ganglion): Pancoast tumour, carotid and aortic aneurysm, neck lesions. Third order (postganglionic, to dilator via long ciliary nerve): cluster headache, ICA dissection, otitis media, cavernous sinus mass. (Book p9)

questions.sec: Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
questions.q: A 58-year-old diabetic presents with Horner's syndrome; MRI shows a lateral medullary infarct (Wallenberg syndrome). The book places this lesion at which neuron order?
opts: The neuromuscular junction of the dilator
questions.exp: Wallenberg syndrome and syringomyelia, brainstem lesions and diabetic autonomic neuropathy are listed under the first-order (central) neuron, hypothalamus to ciliospinal centre (C8-T1). (Book p9)

questions.sec: Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
questions.q: The book's HI MAPLE mnemonic lists the clinical features of Horner's syndrome. All of the following belong to it EXCEPT:
opts: Relative enophthalmos from the lid position
questions.exp: HI MAPLE: Heterochromia Iridis, Inferior eyelid elevation, Miosis, Anhydrosis, Ptosis, Loss of ciliospinal reflex, Relative Enophthalmos. (Book p9)

questions.sec: Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
questions.q: Which statement about Horner's syndrome features is FALSE per the book?
opts: Ptosis results from paralysis of Muller's muscle
Miosis results from paralysis of the dilator pupillae
The enophthalmos of Horner's syndrome is a true posterior displacement of the globe
Heterochromia iridis with ipsilateral hypochromia occurs only in congenital Horner's
questions.exp: The book calls the enophthalmos relative — ptosis plus inferior eyelid elevation give a sunken appearance; it is not true enophthalmos. (Book p9)

questions.sec: Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
questions.q: Inferior eyelid elevation in Horner's syndrome is due to paralysis of which muscle?
questions.exp: Inferior eyelid elevation is paralysis of the inferior tarsal muscle, the analogue of Muller's muscle in the upper lid. (Book p9)

questions.sec: Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
questions.q: Loss of which reflex is listed among the clinical features of Horner's syndrome?
questions.exp: HI MAPLE includes loss of the ciliospinal reflex among Horner's features. (Book p9)

questions.sec: Diagnosis of Horner's syndrome — pharmacological tests
questions.q: Which two structures does the book credit with elevation of the eyelid?
opts: Muller's muscle (superior tarsal) and LPS supplied by CN III
Orbicularis oculi (lid closure) and levator palpebrae inferioris
questions.exp: The note pairs Muller's muscle / superior tarsal muscle with LPS (supplied by CN III) as the elevators of the eyelid. (Book p10)

questions.sec: Diagnosis of Horner's syndrome — pharmacological tests
questions.q: Which statement about the cocaine test for Horner's syndrome is FALSE?
opts: A normal pupil dilates because NE rises in the cleft
In Horner's there is no NE in the cleft, so no dilatation occurs
Failure to dilate after cocaine excludes Horner's syndrome
questions.exp: Cocaine test: blockade of NE reuptake dilates a normal pupil; in Horner's no NE is released, so there is no dilatation — failure to dilate confirms, not excludes, the syndrome. (Book p10)

questions.sec: Diagnosis of Horner's syndrome — pharmacological tests
questions.q: Fill up: with 1% apraclonidine, a normal eye keeps ______ selectivity (miosis), whereas Horner's shows denervation hypersensitivity of α1 receptors and dilates.
questions.exp: Apraclonidine (α agonist): normal selectivity α2 (miosis) > α1; in Horner's denervation hypersensitivity of α1 receptors (mushrooming) reverses selectivity to α1 > α2, dilating the pupil. (Book p10)

questions.sec: Diagnosis of Horner's syndrome — pharmacological tests
questions.q: To localise a confirmed Horner's syndrome the book uses 1% amphetamine (hydroxyamphetamine). No dilatation of the pupil after the test places the lesion:
questions.exp: Hydroxyamphetamine promotes release of NE into the post-synaptic cleft: dilatation means central or preganglionic disease, while no dilatation means the post-ganglionic (final) pathway is affected — post-ganglionic HS. (Book p10)

questions.sec: Diagnosis of Horner's syndrome — pharmacological tests
questions.q: A patient with right-eye ptosis and a smaller right pupil dilates after hydroxyamphetamine. Per the book's localisation tree, the lesion lies in:
opts: The neuromuscular junction of Muller's muscle
questions.exp: Dilatation of the pupil after the amphetamine test indicates a central pathway (central HS) or preganglionic pathway (preganglionic HS) lesion; only absence of dilatation localises post-ganglionically. (Book p10)

questions.sec: Diagnosis of Horner's syndrome — pharmacological tests
questions.q: The photograph captioned in the Horner's section describes which combination?
opts: Absolute enophthalmos with left eye ptosis
questions.exp: The clinical photograph is captioned 'Relative enophthalmos with right eye ptosis'. (Book p10)

questions.sec: Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
questions.q: The book's ITS COMB list gives causes of mydriasis. All of the following belong to it EXCEPT:
questions.exp: ITS COMB (mydriasis): Internal ophthalmoplegia, Tonic pupil, Sympathomimetics, Closure angle glaucoma, Oculomotor 3rd nerve palsy, Mydriatics, Belladonna poisoning; organophosphates belong to the miosis list. (Book p11)

questions.sec: Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
questions.q: The HI COPS list gives causes of miosis. All of the following belong to it EXCEPT:
questions.exp: HI COPS (miosis): Horner's, Hemorrhage (pontine), Iridocyclitis, Clonidine, Carbolic acid, Organophosphates/Opioids, Parasympathomimetics, Sleep/Sedatives; tropicamide is a mydriatic in the ITS COMB list. (Book p11)

questions.sec: Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
questions.q: Aqueous humour is secreted by which part of the uvea?
opts: Pars plana of the ciliary body
questions.exp: Ciliary body functions: secretion of aqueous through the ciliary processes. (Book p11)

questions.sec: Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
questions.q: The book prefers the pars plana as the site of entry into the vitreous cavity because:
opts: It is the thickest uveal tissue of the eye
It secretes the vitreous gel directly
It contains the ciliary muscles of accommodation
questions.exp: Pars plana is the site of entry into the vitreous cavity because relative avascularity reduces the chances of bleeding. (Book p11)

questions.sec: Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
questions.q: Which statement about accommodation per the book is FALSE?
opts: Accommodation tightens the zonules to flatten the lens
Contraction of the ciliary muscles increases the power of the lens
questions.exp: Accommodation = contraction of ciliary muscles → increased lens power with relaxation of zonules, helping near vision; zonular tightening belongs to the relaxed (far-vision) state. (Book p11)

questions.sec: Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
questions.q: The book lists three components of the near reflex. All of the following are components EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Components of the near reflex: accommodation, convergence (inward movement of both eyes) and miosis. (Book p11)

questions.sec: Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
questions.q: Match the visual state with its lens-zonule configuration — 1) Far vision (relaxed state) 2) Near vision with accommodation … A) Ciliary muscles contracted with reduced ring diameter, zonules slack, increased curvature of the anterior surface, increased A-P diameter and increased lens power B) Ciliary muscles relaxed, zonules tense, flat anterior surface
opts: Zonules are tense in both states
questions.exp: The two figures: far vision shows relaxed ciliary muscles with tense zonules and a flat anterior surface; near vision shows contracted muscles (reduced ring diameter), slack zonules, increased anterior curvature, increased A-P diameter and increased lens power. (Book p11)

questions.sec: Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
questions.q: Fill up: presbyopia is the ______ insufficiency of accommodation, producing difficulty with near vision.
questions.exp: Presbyopia is defined as physiological insufficiency of accommodation causing difficulty in near vision such as using phones or reading newspaper. (Book p12)

questions.sec: Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
questions.q: Per the book's age rule for presbyopic correction, the add power required at 50 years of age is:
questions.exp: At 40 years +1 D is required and every additional 5 years adds +0.5 D: 45 years +1.5 D, 50 years +2 D. (Book p12)

questions.sec: Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
questions.q: The book states presbyopia typically begins around which age?
questions.exp: Onset of presbyopia: around 40 years of age. (Book p12)

questions.sec: Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
questions.q: The book's preference order for presbyopic spectacles is:
questions.exp: Rx: convex (+) spectacles with the preference progressives > D-bifocals >>> executive lenses; power depends on age. (Book p12)

questions.sec: Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
questions.q: Match the spectacle type with its book description — 1) Monofocal 2) Progressive lenses 3) D-bifocals 4) Executive bifocals … A) Cosmetically unappealing with no provision for intermediate vision B) Power restricted to a central hourglass configuration with no power in the peripheries, giving a restricted field of view C) Pupil bisected by the line between the lenses; obsolete except in paediatric aphakia D) Cosmetically appealing with seamless transition, covering near, intermediate and far vision
questions.exp: Monofocal (only near-vision patients): power restricted to centre hourglass, no power in peripheries, restricted field of view. Progressives: seamless, cosmetically appealing, cover near/intermediate/far. D-bifocals: cosmetically unappealing, no intermediate provision. Executive bifocals: pupil bisected by the line between lenses, obsolete except paediatric aphakia. (Book p12)

questions.sec: Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
questions.q: A 46-year-old tailor who has never worn glasses complains that threading a needle and reading his phone have become difficult, while distance vision is fine. The book's first-line correction for him is:
questions.exp: Patients only needing near-vision lenses (no existing distance glasses) are given monofocal spectacles; progressives/bifocals are for patients already using glasses for far vision. (Book p12)

questions.sec: Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
questions.q: Spasm of accommodation produces which functional loss, and under what name?
questions.exp: Spasm of accommodation is a continuous state of contraction of the ciliary muscles causing loss of far vision, labelled pseudomyopia. (Book p12)

questions.sec: Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
questions.q: The book treats spasm of accommodation with cycloplegia. Which drug group does it list?
opts: Miotics — pilocarpine and carbachol eye drops
Beta blockers — timolol eye drops twice daily
questions.exp: Treatment is cycloplegia (relaxation of ciliary muscles) with drugs: mydriatics and cycloplegics — atropine, homatropine, cyclopentolate. (Book p12)

units.title: Components of the uvea and the anatomy of the iris
units.guide: The uvea table splits iris plus ciliary-body pars plicata into anterior uvea (anterior uveitis), pars plana into intermediate uvea (intermediate uveitis) and choroid into posterior uvea (posterior uveitis). The iris is highly vascular, pigmented d/t melanocytes and of variable thickness; its thickest part is the collarette (boundary of pupillary and ciliary zones) and its thinnest part the root — the site of iridodialysis. Sphincter pupillae (miosis, parasympathetic inhibitory via CN III, final short ciliary nerve) opposes dilator pupillae (mydriasis, sympathetic excitatory: hypothalamus → C8-T1 ciliospinal centre → superior cervical ganglion → long ciliary nerve), with Pancoast tumour resection flagged as a risk to the SCG fibres.

units.title: Oculomotor branches, Horner's syndrome — neuron orders and HI MAPLE features
units.guide: The oculomotor nerve's superior branch supplies superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris; the inferior branch supplies inferior rectus and inferior oblique. Horner's syndrome is oculosympathetic palsy. First-order (central) causes: brainstem lesions, syringomyelia, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, Wallenberg syndrome; second-order (preganglionic): Pancoast tumour, carotid and aortic aneurysm, neck lesions; third-order (postganglionic): cluster headache, ICA dissection, otitis media, cavernous sinus mass. Features run by the mnemonic HI MAPLE — heterochromia iridis (ipsilateral hypochromia, congenital cases only), inferior eyelid elevation (inferior tarsal muscle), miosis, anhydrosis, ptosis (Muller's muscle), loss of ciliospinal reflex and relative enophthalmos.

units.title: Diagnosing and localising Horner's syndrome — cocaine, apraclonidine and amphetamine tests
units.guide: Muller's (superior tarsal) muscle and the CN III-supplied LPS elevate the eyelid. Detection: the cocaine test blocks NE reuptake — a normal pupil dilates, Horner's does not (no NE released); 1% apraclonidine keeps normal α2 > α1 selectivity but dilates Horner's through α1 denervation hypersensitivity (mushrooming). Localisation: 1% amphetamine (hydroxyamphetamine) releases NE into the cleft — dilatation places the lesion centrally or preganglionically, no dilatation post-ganglionically. The section photograph shows relative enophthalmos with right eye ptosis.

units.title: Pupil-size mnemonics, ciliary body functions and the mechanics of accommodation
units.guide: Mydriasis causes run ITS COMB (internal ophthalmoplegia, tonic pupil/Holmes-Adie, sympathomimetics, closure-angle glaucoma, oculomotor palsy, mydriatics, belladonna poisoning); miosis causes run HI COPS (Horner's, pontine hemorrhage, iridocyclitis, clonidine, carbolic acid, organophosphates/opioids, parasympathomimetics, sleep/sedatives). The ciliary body secretes aqueous through its ciliary processes, offers the relatively avascular pars plana as the vitreous entry site, and accomplishes accommodation by contracting its muscles (↑ lens power) while relaxing the zonules. The near reflex = accommodation + convergence + miosis; far vision keeps muscles relaxed with tense zonules and a flat anterior surface, near vision contracts the muscles (↓ ring diameter), slackens zonules and raises anterior curvature, A-P diameter and lens power.

units.title: Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia, spectacle types and spasm of accommodation
units.guide: Presbyopia is physiological insufficiency of accommodation with onset around 40 years; correction is convex (+) spectacles, +1 D at 40 years and +0.5 D for every further 5 years, preferring progressives > D-bifocals >>> executive lenses. Monofocals suit patients needing only near vision (central hourglass power, restricted field), progressives give seamless near-intermediate-far coverage, D-bifocals lack intermediate vision and executive bifocals bisect the pupil and survive only in paediatric aphakia. Spasm of accommodation — continuous ciliary contraction — causes loss of far vision (pseudomyopia) and is treated with cycloplegic mydriatics: atropine, homatropine, cyclopentolate.
